lead: A stiffened panel is skin plus stringers. In compression the thin skin buckles between stringers before the stringers fail. The buckled skin is not useless, but it carries load mainly near the stringers. Engineers replace the real stress distribution by an effective width of skin working at the stringer stress. This keeps hand calculations simple. The idea is used in wing and fuselage compression panels, where weight must be low but the skin must still contribute. It is also the first step in boom-panel idealisation for bending and shear flow.
prereq: You need: 6.3 for plate buckling, and Unit 5 for shear flow, booms and panels.

blocks.text: A stiffened panel has a thin skin riveted or bonded to stringers. The stringers run along the load direction. The distance between two stringers is the pitch p. Under compression, the skin is a plate supported along the stringers. It buckles locally at a stress below the stress that would fail the stringer. After buckling, the skin cannot carry the same stress everywhere. The middle of each bay deflects out of plane and sheds load. The skin near a stringer is held straight by the stringer and carries more load. The stress is high at the stringer and low at mid-bay. This non-uniform stress is hard to use in a simple beam calculation. The effective width method replaces it with a smaller width of skin at the uniform stringer stress. That artificial width carries the same load as the real buckled skin. This is why a stiffened panel can be lighter than an unstiffened sheet that carries the same compressive load. The method is used for wing upper surface panels, fuselage crown panels and tail compression panels.

sections.h3: Effective width formula and boom area

blocks.text: The effective width on each side of a stringer is b<sub>eff</sub>. A common design form is the formula below. It applies after the skin has buckled locally between stringers.

blocks.where: b<sub>eff</sub> is the effective sheet width on each side of the stringer in mm or m; C is a dimensionless effective-width constant; t is skin thickness in the same length unit; E is Young's modulus in MPa or Pa; σ is the compressive stress at the stringer in the same unit as E.

blocks.text: The example uses C = 1.9, a common value for a simply supported sheet. Design charts give C for other edge supports and stress levels. Use E and σ in the same units. The effective width is per side. It must not exceed half the pitch p/2; if b<sub>eff</sub> exceeds p/2, the effective zones from adjacent stringers meet; then count the whole bay width p as effective, because the applied stress is no higher than the local buckling stress of the skin. The stiffener plus its effective skin is treated as a boom in Unit 5.

blocks.where: A<sub>eff</sub> is the effective area per stringer in mm² or m²; A<sub>st</sub> is the stringer cross-sectional area; b<sub>eff</sub> is the effective width on one side; t is skin thickness; the factor 2 counts the skin on both sides of the stringer.

items: Find the skin compressive stress σ at the stringer for the load case.
Choose C for the edge support and stress level.
Put t, E and σ into consistent units.
Compute b<sub>eff</sub> and limit it to p/2 on each side.
Compute A<sub>eff</sub> for the stringer plus effective skin.
Use A<sub>eff</sub> in the boom idealisation, then check the stringer itself for local buckling and crippling in 6.5.

blocks.text: The effective width formula is for uniform compression and local skin buckling. It does not cover shear lag. Shear lag is the delay of shear stress transfer between skin and stringers. Stringer stress therefore changes over a length instead of jumping at once. It matters near cut-outs, wing roots and concentrated loads. For a closed box, shear lag analysis is a separate problem. The method also assumes the stringer does not cripple first; check local buckling and crippling in 6.5. For composite stiffened panels the same idea exists, but stiffness is directional; see 6.7 and 6.8. In a real panel, skin buckling may be stable and the panel can carry more load after buckling. The effective width is a strength estimate, not a full post-buckling analysis.

examples.question: A stiffened panel has stringer area 200 mm², skin thickness 1.5 mm and E = 70 GPa. At skin stress 100 MPa the effective-width constant is 1.9. Find b<sub>eff</sub> on each side and the effective area per stringer.
steps: List the data: A<sub>st</sub> = 200 mm², t = 1.5 mm, E = 70 GPa = 70 000 MPa, σ = 100 MPa, C = 1.9.
Check the modulus-to-stress ratio: E/σ = 70 000/100 = 700. It is dimensionless.
Compute the effective width: b<sub>eff</sub> = C t √(E/σ) = 1.9 × 1.5 mm × 26.46 = 75.4 mm on each side.
No pitch is given here, so the p/2 limit cannot be checked; with p = 60 mm the limit would be 30 mm per side and b<sub>eff</sub> would need cutting to 30 mm.
Compute the effective area: A<sub>eff</sub> = A<sub>st</sub> + 2 b<sub>eff</sub> t = 200 + 2 × 75.4 × 1.5 = 200 + 226.2 = 426.2 mm².
examples.answer: The effective width is 75.4 mm on each side of the stringer, and the effective area per stringer is 426.2 mm².
examples.check:
import math
C = 1.9
t = 1.5
E = 70000.0
sigma = 100.0
A_st = 200.0
b_eff = C * t * math.sqrt(E / sigma)
A_eff = A_st + 2 * b_eff * t
print(round(b_eff, 1))
print(round(A_eff, 1))

traps: Using the full pitch p as effective skin width after buckling. Only b<sub>eff</sub> on each side is added.
Adding b<sub>eff</sub> once when the stringer has skin on both sides, or twice at a free edge. Count the sheet surfaces correctly.
Putting σ in MPa and E in GPa in b<sub>eff</sub> = C t √(E/σ). Make E and σ the same unit.
Using yield stress in the formula no matter what load the panel carries. Use the actual stiffener stress at that load case.
Calling b<sub>eff</sub> the stiffener pitch. b<sub>eff</sub> is a reduced width; pitch is the spacing between stringers.

quiz.q: Define effective sheet width in one sentence.
quiz.a: It is the reduced width of buckled skin, at stringer stress, that carries the same load as the actual non-uniform skin.

quiz.q: Why does the skin at mid-bay carry little load after buckling?
quiz.a: It deflects out of plane, so its membrane stiffness in compression drops. The skin near stiffeners stays straighter and carries more load.

quiz.q: A sheet has t = 2 mm, E = 72 GPa, σ = 120 MPa and C = 1.8. Find b<sub>eff</sub> per side.
A stringer has A<sub>st</sub> = 250 mm², skin t = 2 mm and b<sub>eff</sub> = 40 mm per side. Find A<sub>eff</sub>.
A panel has pitch p = 60 mm. The formula gives b<sub>eff</sub> = 40 mm. What is wrong and what do you use?
quiz.a: b<sub>eff</sub> exceeds p/2 = 30 mm, so the effective zones overlap. Limit each side to 30 mm and treat the full sheet as effective.

quiz.q: Why can two panels with the same skin thickness and stringer area have different A<sub>eff</sub>?
quiz.a: C, stringer stress, E, edge support and pitch can differ. The p/2 limit and whether the stringer has one or two sheet sides also change A<sub>eff</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, stiffened-panel post-buckling is checked with finite element models that allow the skin to wrinkle while the stringers remain straight. Effective width remains a quick hand check for preliminary sizing and for checking computer output. In composite wings, the same idea becomes directional because skin stiffness along and across the fibres differs. Search terms: post-buckled stiffened panel, effective width, shear lag, boom idealisation, and composite stiffener run-out.
